Your dynamic arrays spill into populated cells and break. Here's how to fix it permanently.

The fix: Use the @ operator to force a single-cell result when you don't want spill behavior. Or use the # operator to reference the entire spilled range.

=FILTER(SalesData,SalesData[Region]="West")#

The # at the end tells the next formula "use the whole spilled array." Now your downstream formulas update automatically when filter results change.

You're hardcoding tax rates and percentages directly into formulas. This is the #1 cause of Excel errors per two separate academic studies.

The fix: Pull every input into a named cell.

Bad: =Revenue * 0.21
Good: Put 0.21 in cell B2, name it TaxRate, then write =Revenue * TaxRate

When the tax rate changes (and it will), you update ONE cell instead of hunting through 47 formulas.

Drop the hardcoded number you should have separated months ago.

Your Excel file got slow and you don't know why. Here's the diagnosis order.

Press F9. If recalculation takes >2 seconds → you have volatile functions (NOW, TODAY, OFFSET, INDIRECT) doing too much work.

Check Format → Conditional Formatting → Manage Rules. Multiple rules on entire columns = death.

Check Name Manager (Ctrl+F3). Broken named ranges silently destroy performance.

Fix one at a time. Save between each. Most slow files have all three problems.

You're using SUMIF (singular). SUMIFS (plural) does more in one step.

The fix:
Old: =SUMIF(A:A,"West",B:B) with a helper column for month
New: =SUMIFS(B:B, A:A, "West", C:C, "January")

SUMIFS takes unlimited condition pairs. Same with COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MINIFS, MAXIFS. Drop the "S" from your old habits.
